analogy.p: Imagine a school canteen where the food is cooked in one corner, but the queue for it is in another, and some students have lunch money while others do not. Even if the canteen cooks enough food for everyone (like the world producing enough calories), students at the far end may go hungry because they are far from the serving hatch, cannot afford a meal, or the doors are shut (distribution, poverty and conflict). The analogy maps supply to the food cooked, consumption to what students eat, and surplus and deficit to full and empty plates. It breaks down because real resources such as oil are fixed by geology, and the canteen can simply move food around easily whereas real trade of resources is slow, expensive and political.
analogy.t: A school canteen with uneven queues

bullets: **Resource** = anything in the natural environment that people can use to meet their needs; food, water and energy are the three you study.
**Supply** = the amount of a resource that is produced, extracted or made available; **consumption** = the amount actually used by people.
A **surplus** means supply is bigger than demand; a **deficit** means demand is bigger than supply.
Resources are **unevenly distributed**: some regions have plenty, others have almost none, and some people have the resource nearby but cannot afford it.
You only study ONE of food, water or energy in depth, but exam questions on this opening point can ask about any of the three, so learn all three.
Exam questions often give a map, graph or table (for example calorie supply by country) and ask you to describe the pattern or suggest reasons.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to understand that **food, water and energy are fundamental to human development** and that these resources are **not distributed evenly** around the world. You must be able to describe the global pattern of **supply** (how much is produced or available) and **consumption** (how much people actually use), and explain why some places have a **surplus** while others have a **deficit**. The section also asks you to look at the changing demand for and provision of these resources in the UK. Everything later in Section C (food, water, energy, sustainable strategies) builds on this starting idea of inequality.

bullets: **Renewable:** can be replaced naturally within a human lifetime or used without running out, for example **solar, wind, tidal, hydroelectric (HEP), geothermal and biomass energy**.
**Non-renewable (finite):** **coal, oil and natural gas** (the fossil fuels) and uranium; once burned they cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
Fossil fuels formed from the remains of ancient plants and tiny sea creatures, which is why they are found only in certain rock layers and regions.
Food is renewable only if soils stay fertile and water is available; over-farming can turn it into a degraded resource.

Fresh water is renewable through the water cycle, but about **97% of the Earth's water is salty**, and most of the fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, so **less than 1% is easily accessible**.
Link to sustainability: using a resource faster than it renews is **unsustainable** (covered in the later point on strategies).
core.h: What is a resource? Renewable and non-renewable
core.p: A **natural resource** is a material from the environment that has a use for people. Resources are usually split into **renewable** resources, which are replaced naturally or can be used again (water, wind, sunlight, food crops if farmed properly) and **non-renewable** resources, which take millions of years to form and will run out if used (coal, oil, natural gas). This matters for supply because non-renewable resources have a fixed stock, and the places that hold them are decided by geology, not by human choice. Even renewable resources can be over-used, for example if water is taken from a river or aquifer faster than it is replaced.

bullets: **Food** provides the **calories** (energy) and nutrients needed for growth, health, and physical and mental work; a hungry population is less productive and has more illness.
**Water** is needed for **drinking, cooking, hygiene and sanitation**; dirty water spreads diseases such as cholera and typhoid, which keeps children out of school and adults out of work.
Water is also essential for **irrigating crops** and for manufacturing and power generation, so water supply limits both food production and industry.
**Energy** powers factories, machines, farms, transport, hospitals, schools, lighting, heating and communications; economic growth needs a reliable supply.
Electricity access is a development issue: millions of people still have none and rely on **wood, charcoal or dung** for cooking, which is time-consuming and causes indoor air pollution.
Higher levels of development generally mean **higher consumption** of all three resources, which is why richer countries use so much more energy and food per person.
core.h: Why food, water and energy are fundamental to development
core.p: **Development** means the improvement of people's quality of life, often measured by indicators such as the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, life expectancy and income. Food, water and energy are fundamental because without them people cannot stay healthy, work, learn or build an economy. A country where many people are hungry, lack clean water or have no electricity struggles to grow richer, which keeps it in a cycle of poverty. The three resources are also linked to one another, so a shortage of one often causes a shortage of another.

bullets: **Distribution** = where a resource is found; **consumption** = where it is used. These two patterns are often very different.
**Producers** and **consumers** are frequently in different parts of the world, so resources are traded internationally (for example oil moves from the Middle East to Asia and Europe).
High-income countries (HICs) contain a small share of the world's population but use a large share of the world's energy and food resources.
Low-income countries (LICs) have low consumption per person, often because people cannot afford resources or the infrastructure to deliver them is missing.
Newly emerging economies (NEEs), such as China and India, now have rapidly **rising consumption** as their populations grow richer.
Always use the phrase **per person (per capita)** when comparing countries, because a big country can use a lot in total but little per person.
core.h: The key idea: supply and consumption are uneven
core.p: The most important idea in this point is that **global inequality** exists in both how much of a resource a place has and how much its people use. Some countries have large amounts of a resource but use little (for example a poor country with oil it cannot yet extract), while others use far more than they produce (for example Japan, which has very few fossil fuels and imports almost all of its oil and gas). Some resources, like food, are produced in enough quantity worldwide to feed everyone, yet hunger continues because of problems of access, poverty and transport. When you describe a pattern, always mention both the **supply** side and the **consumption** side and use data to show the contrast.

bullets: **Calorie supply per person** is the commonest indicator used on maps; darker shades on a choropleth map usually show higher supply.
**Surplus areas:** North America, most of Europe, Australia and New Zealand, parts of South America such as Argentina and Brazil.
**Deficit areas:** large parts of sub-Saharan Africa (for example the Horn of Africa and the Sahel), parts of South Asia and some countries in conflict such as Yemen.
The world produces **enough calories to feed everyone**, so global hunger is mainly a problem of **distribution, access and poverty**, not of total production.
Food surplus can lead to **over-consumption** and health problems such as **obesity**, while deficit leads to **undernutrition**; both are forms of malnutrition.
Exam tip: when describing a map, quote the **highest and lowest values** and name regions, then point out **anomalies** (for example a poor country with unusually high supply).
core.h: Global food supply: surplus and deficit
core.p: Food supply is often measured in **calories per person per day**. The average adult needs roughly **2,000 to 2,500 kilocalories (kcal) per day**, depending on age, sex and activity. Many HICs, such as the USA and countries in Europe, have a supply well above this level (often **3,300 to 3,800 kcal**), meaning a **food surplus**, while some countries in **sub-Saharan Africa** and parts of South Asia have an average supply close to or below the amount needed, meaning a **food deficit**. Averages hide inequality inside countries, so even a country with a surplus can have hungry people.

bullets: **Climate:** reliable rainfall and a long growing season increase yields; **drought** or flooding can destroy crops.
**Soils and relief:** deep fertile soils on flat land are ideal; steep slopes and thin soils limit farming.
**Wealth and technology:** HICs use machinery, hybrid seeds, irrigation and fertiliser (**high yields per hectare**); LICs may use hand tools and rain-fed farming.
**Infrastructure:** poor roads, lack of cold storage and weak markets mean much food is **wasted before it is eaten** in LICs, while in HICs waste happens more at shops and homes.
**Conflict and political instability** disrupt farming and trade, so food deficits are often found in war zones.
**Trade:** wealthy countries can **import** food to cover shortages, whereas poor countries often lack the money to do so.
core.h: Why food supply is distributed unevenly
core.p: The pattern of food supply is explained by a mixture of **physical** and **human** factors. Physical factors include climate, soils and relief: places with warm temperatures, enough rainfall and fertile soil, such as the mid-latitude plains of the USA or Ukraine, can grow large amounts of food, while deserts, mountains and very cold areas cannot. Human factors include wealth, technology, political stability and trade: rich countries can afford irrigation, machinery, fertiliser and storage, and can import food they cannot grow. Poorer countries often depend on rain-fed farming and have weak transport systems, so harvests are smaller and food is lost before it reaches markets.

bullets: **Water surplus:** high rainfall and low population, for example Canada, Norway, Brazil (the Amazon) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
**Water deficit:** low rainfall and/or high demand, for example Saudi Arabia, Libya, Egypt, parts of India and northern China.
The distribution of **fresh water** matches neither population nor demand, so the biggest populations (such as India and China) face large local shortages.
**Agriculture uses about 70% of all fresh water withdrawn** worldwide, so water supply strongly affects food supply.
Water scarcity can also be **local and seasonal**: monsoon countries have plenty in the wet season and shortages in the dry season.
Remember that a **surplus does not guarantee access**: millions of people in water-rich countries still lack clean drinking water.
core.h: Global water supply: surplus and deficit
core.p: Water supply is usually described as the amount of **renewable fresh water available per person per year**, measured in cubic metres (m3). The common thresholds are **above 1,700 m3 per person per year = adequate**, **below 1,700 = water stress**, **below 1,000 = water scarcity** and **below 500 = absolute scarcity**. A **water surplus** exists where supply exceeds demand, as in much of Canada, northern Europe, Russia, Brazil and parts of South-East Asia, while a **water deficit** is found in the Middle East, North Africa, parts of Central and South Asia, and some regions of Australia and the USA. Roughly two billion people live in areas of high water stress.

bullets: **Physical scarcity:** low rainfall, high evaporation, over-use of rivers and aquifers, for example the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa.
**Economic scarcity:** inadequate investment in dams, pipes, wells and sanitation, for example many rural parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
**Population growth and urbanisation** increase demand and can push a water-adequate area into stress.
**Pollution** from industry, farming and sewage reduces the amount of usable water even where the total volume is high.
**Climate change** is altering rainfall patterns, with some regions becoming drier and others wetter.
Higher-tier thinking: the same country can be both (for example India has both over-extraction of groundwater and unequal access to piped supply).
core.p: Geographers separate two causes of water shortage. **Physical water scarcity** happens when there is simply not enough water to meet demand, usually because the climate is arid or because the population is too large for the available supply. **Economic water scarcity** happens when water exists in the environment but people cannot use it because they lack the money, technology or infrastructure (wells, pipes, treatment works) to collect, clean and deliver it. Much of sub-Saharan Africa suffers economic scarcity, while the Middle East and North Africa mainly suffer physical scarcity. Using these terms in answers shows you understand that the same shortage can have different causes.

bullets: **Energy producers** are not always rich: some very large exporters (such as Nigeria) still have large numbers of people living in poverty.
**Energy exporters** include the Middle East, Russia, Norway and Australia; **big importers** include Japan, South Korea, much of Europe and, increasingly, India and China.
**Energy mix** = the proportion of each energy source used by a country; it differs hugely (France relies heavily on nuclear; Norway on HEP; Poland on coal).
Renewable potential is not the same as renewable use: a sunny but poor country may not afford solar farms and grid connections.
**Transport and pipelines** matter: gas is moved by pipeline or liquefied (LNG) by ship, so supply can be disrupted by politics or conflict.
Link to Paper 1: plate boundaries and climate (tectonics, climate zones) help explain why geothermal and HEP are found where they are.
core.h: Global energy supply: where energy resources are found
core.p: The distribution of energy resources is controlled mainly by **geology and climate**. **Oil and natural gas** are concentrated in particular sedimentary basins, most famously in the **Middle East** (Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Qatar), but also in Russia, the USA, Canada, Nigeria, Venezuela and the North Sea. **Coal** is mined in China, India, the USA, Indonesia, Australia and Russia. Renewable potential also varies: **geothermal** energy is best near plate boundaries (Iceland), **solar** energy in sunny, cloud-free regions near the tropics, **wind** on exposed coasts and uplands, and **hydroelectric power (HEP)** in wet, mountainous areas with steep river valleys (Norway, Brazil, Canada). Fossil fuels still supply about **80% of the world's primary energy**.

bullets: **Per capita consumption** is the best way to compare; **total consumption** can mislead because of population size (India has low per capita use but a huge population).
**HICs:** high but, in many cases, now **stable or falling** because of energy efficiency, a shift to services and de-industrialisation.
**NEEs:** consumption **rising rapidly** because of industrialisation, urban growth and rising incomes; often powered by coal.
**LICs:** low consumption; **energy poverty** is common, meaning people cannot get affordable, reliable, modern energy.
Rising consumption leads to higher **carbon dioxide emissions** and **climate change** unless the energy mix includes more renewables.
Because demand is rising faster than supply in some regions, **energy security** (having reliable, affordable supplies) is a major political concern.
core.p: Energy consumption per person is closely linked to **wealth and level of development**. Industrialised and wealthy countries such as the USA, Canada, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Norway and Iceland use very large amounts of energy per person because of widespread car use, heating and cooling, large homes and energy-hungry industry. LICs use far less because fewer people have electricity, vehicles or appliances; roughly **700 million people have no access to electricity** and over **two billion rely on wood, charcoal or dung** for cooking. NEEs such as China and India are the fastest-growing consumers, and China is now the world's largest user of energy overall.

bullets: **Food needs water:** it takes thousands of litres of water to produce one kilogram of beef compared with far less for wheat.
**Food needs energy:** modern farming uses diesel for machinery, and fertiliser production uses large quantities of natural gas.
**Energy needs water:** thermal power stations (coal, gas, nuclear) use huge volumes of water for cooling.
**Water needs energy:** pumping, desalination and treatment plants are energy-intensive; desalination is very costly in energy terms.
**Biofuels** show a conflict: growing crops for fuel can reduce land available for food and raise food prices.
Exam use: when asked to explain why resource problems are connected, give one clear chain such as 'drought reduces HEP output and crop yields at the same time'.
core.h: The links between food, water and energy
core.p: Food, water and energy are **interdependent**, sometimes called the **water-energy-food nexus**. Growing food needs water (for irrigation) and energy (for machinery, fertiliser production, processing and transport). Producing energy needs water (for cooling power stations, for HEP, for extracting oil) and sometimes land (for biofuel crops). Treating and pumping water needs energy. This means a shortage in one resource can cause shortages in the others, and a strategy that boosts one resource may harm another.

bullets: **Resource security** means having a reliable supply of a resource in the quantity and quality needed; **food security**, **water security** and **energy security** are the three forms.
Countries dependent on one supplier are vulnerable to **price shocks** and political disputes (for example European reliance on imported gas).
**Resource nationalism:** governments may control or limit exports of their own resources to protect their people or raise income.
**Globalisation** has increased resource trade but also increased the risk that a shock in one place affects supply and prices everywhere.
**Virtual water** = the water used to produce goods that are traded; countries short of water import water-intensive food rather than grow it.
Evaluating tip: trade can reduce shortages, but it only helps people who can **afford** the imports.
core.p: Because resources are distributed unevenly, **international trade** is needed to move them from places of surplus to places of deficit. Wealthy countries can afford to buy food, water-intensive goods and energy on world markets, which protects them against local shortages, while poorer countries often cannot. This inequality means that price rises (for example when oil prices surge or a harvest fails) affect LICs most severely. Countries try to protect themselves through **resource security**, for example by storing food and fuel, building reservoirs, and diversifying where they buy from.

bullets: **Changing UK diet and lifestyle:** more ready meals, imported fruit and vegetables, organic and ethnic foods; shoppers expect everything all year round.
**Food miles:** the distance food travels from farm to consumer; imported goods increase food miles and carbon emissions.
**UK water demand** has increased because of population growth, more single-person households, and appliances such as dishwashers and washing machines (about 140 to 150 litres per person per day).
**Water transfer schemes** move water from surplus areas (Wales, the Lake District, Kielder in Northumberland) to deficit areas (the Midlands, London and the South East).
**UK energy mix** has changed from mainly coal to gas, nuclear and a growing share of **wind, solar and biomass**, with renewables now providing a large and rising share of electricity.
**Issues created:** reliance on imports (energy security), rising bills, carbon emissions, and pressure on southern water supplies in dry summers.
core.h: The UK: changing demand and provision of resources
core.p: The UK shows how a developed country's resource needs change over time. The UK is highly urbanised with a population of around 67 to 68 million, and has become increasingly dependent on **imports** of food and energy. **Food:** the UK produces roughly 60% of the food it consumes, so around 40% is imported, because of year-round demand for foods that cannot be grown here (such as bananas, coffee and out-of-season fruit) and changing diets. **Water:** the **north and west** receive most of the rain and have a **surplus**, while the **south and east** are drier and densely populated, so they suffer a **deficit**, and water is transferred by pipelines and aqueducts (for example from the Elan Valley in Wales to Birmingham). **Energy:** the UK was self-sufficient in the 1990s thanks to **North Sea oil and gas**, but production peaked around the late 1990s and early 2000s and the UK became a **net importer** of energy; coal use has fallen to almost nothing (the last coal power station closed in 2024) while **renewables, especially wind**, have grown rapidly.

bullets: **Describe the pattern:** start with the overall trend (for example 'consumption is highest in North America and lowest in Africa'), then give two figures with units.
**Use the key:** check what the shades or units mean (kcal per person per day, m3 per person per year, kWh per person).
**Compare:** use words like 'whereas', 'in contrast' and 'twice as much as' with calculated differences.
**Calculate:** know how to work out percentage differences and per-person figures from totals (see the worked examples).
**Anomalies:** mention places that break the pattern, such as Iceland (low population, huge geothermal and HEP energy use per person) or oil-rich but poor countries.
**Suggest reasons:** link to climate, geology, wealth, technology, population and political stability, and always say which factor is most important and why.
core.h: Interpreting maps and graphs on global resource distribution
core.p: Exam questions on this point nearly always include a resource stimulus: a world choropleth map, a bar chart of calories, a scatter graph of energy use against income, or a table of water per person. The marks are earned by **using data**, comparing places and giving reasons. A strong description has a general statement, specific named places with figures, and an anomaly. A strong explanation uses linked reasoning: a cause, a consequence and a link to development or wealth.

exam: **1 mark:** give a definition or read a single value from a map or graph (for example 'State what is meant by a water deficit'). Write one precise phrase and include units for any figure.
**2 marks: 'Suggest one reason...'** make a point and develop it with 'because' or 'so' (for example 'Rain is low in the Middle East, so there is little river water available').
**'Describe' (usually 2 to 4 marks):** state the pattern, add named places and data (with units), and add an anomaly; no explanations are needed.
**'Explain' (usually 4 marks):** build chains of reasoning: point, because, so/which means. Aim for two developed reasons rather than four undeveloped ones.
**Use command words:** 'Assess' and 'To what extent' (6 or 9 marks, levelled) need both sides plus a justified judgement at the end.
**Graph and map skills:** check the key and units, quote values, compare with calculated differences, and mention the highest, lowest and anomalies.
**Calculations:** show the working (for example per person = total divided by population); a correct answer with no units may lose a mark.
**Use exact terminology:** surplus, deficit, supply, consumption, per capita, physical and economic water scarcity, energy mix, energy security.
**Link the three resources** where possible (water for food, energy for water) to show higher-level understanding.
**Include the UK** when the question asks about changing demand or provision: mention imports, North Sea decline, north-west surplus and south-east deficit, and the shift to renewables.

mistakes.r: Name specific regions or countries (for example the Horn of Africa, the Sahel) and qualify with data; Africa also has areas of surplus.
mistakes.w: Saying 'Africa has no food or water' or treating Africa as one country.

mistakes.r: Compare **per capita** figures; large populations such as India and China use a lot in total but less per person than the USA.
mistakes.w: Describing total consumption without saying per person.

mistakes.r: The world produces enough calories for everyone; hunger results from poverty, poor distribution, conflict and waste.
mistakes.w: Saying the world does not produce enough food.

mistakes.r: Distinguish **physical** scarcity (not enough water) from **economic** scarcity (no money or infrastructure to use the water that exists).
mistakes.w: Writing 'water scarcity is just lack of rain'.

mistakes.r: Quote named places and values with units, give the overall trend, and mention at least one anomaly.
mistakes.w: Only describing the map ('some places are dark and some light').

mistakes.r: Having a resource does not guarantee development; poor countries can have oil or water but lack money, technology or stability to use it.
mistakes.w: Confusing a resource surplus with wealth.

mistakes.r: Renewable means it can be replaced; sustainable means used in a way that does not harm future generations. A renewable resource can be used unsustainably.
Rain is unevenly distributed: the north and west have a surplus, the south and east (where most people live) have a deficit.
mistakes.w: Saying the UK has no water problems because it rains a lot.

summary: You must know that food, water and energy are fundamental to human development and that their supply (what is produced or available) and consumption (what is used) are distributed very unevenly around the world, creating surpluses in some places and deficits in others. You also need to explain the reasons for these patterns and understand how demand and provision of these resources have changed in the UK. This underpins the whole resource management section of Paper 2.

terms.d: Anything in the natural environment that people can use to meet their needs.
A resource that is replaced naturally or can be used repeatedly without running out, such as wind, solar or water.
A resource that takes millions of years to form and will run out if used, such as coal, oil and natural gas.
The amount of a resource that is produced, extracted or made available.
The amount of a resource that is actually used by people.
When supply of a resource is greater than demand.
When demand for a resource is greater than the supply available.
The amount of food energy, measured in kilocalories (kcal), consumed per person per day.
When annual water supply falls below about 1,700 cubic metres per person and demand begins to exceed supply.
A shortage of water because there is not enough available in the environment to meet demand.
A shortage caused by lack of money, technology or infrastructure to collect, treat and deliver water that exists.
The proportion of each energy source (coal, oil, gas, nuclear, renewables) used by a country.
Having an uninterrupted supply of energy that is reliable, affordable and sufficient for a country's needs.
When people cannot access or afford enough modern, reliable energy for their basic needs.
The improvement in quality of life and standard of living of a country's people, measured by indicators such as HDI.
Per person; used to compare countries fairly regardless of population size.
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten.
Moving water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit using pipes, canals or aqueducts.

worked.ans: 750 m3 per person per year, which is **water scarcity** (below 1,000 m3 but above the 500 m3 absolute scarcity level).
worked.q: A country has 60 billion cubic metres of renewable fresh water each year and a population of 80 million. Calculate the water available per person per year and state what category of water availability this is. (3 marks)
steps: Water per person = total water divided by population.
60 000 000 000 divided by 80 000 000 = 750 cubic metres per person per year.
Compare with thresholds: 750 is below 1,000 but above 500.

worked.q: Country A has an average food supply of 3,400 kcal per person per day. Country B has 2,100 kcal. Calculate how much more food energy per person Country A has than Country B as a percentage of Country B's supply. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: Water supply is controlled by climate, because hot desert areas such as the Middle East have very low rainfall and high evaporation, so there is little surface water and a **physical deficit**. In contrast, places such as Canada and Brazil have high rainfall and low population density, so supply exceeds demand, creating a **surplus**. Demand also matters: large populations and irrigated farming in northern China use more water than rainfall provides, so a deficit occurs even though some water exists. Finally, many LICs have **economic scarcity** because they cannot afford dams, pipes or treatment plants, so people lack water despite it being present.
worked.q: Explain why some parts of the world have a water deficit while other parts have a water surplus. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1 (physical): climate: low rainfall and high evaporation in hot deserts such as the Middle East means little river water, whereas high rainfall in equatorial and cool temperate areas fills rivers and aquifers.
Point 2 (human demand): large or growing populations, irrigation and industry use large amounts, so even areas with moderate rainfall (for example northern China) can have a deficit.
Point 3 (economic): some places lack the money and infrastructure for wells, pipes and treatment, so water that exists cannot be used (economic scarcity).
